reports.topic: Free, commercially shippable music sources for a Cold War grand strategy game (1950s orchestral, jazz noir, ambient tension)

findings.name: FreePD.com — SHUT DOWN; use the Internet Archive mirror
findings.detail: Major finding: FreePD.com is offline as of 2025/2026 — https://freepd.com/ now shows only a closure notice ('After 17 years... officially taken the service offline'). The catalog (Kevin MacLeod's CC0 re-releases, Bryan Teoh, Rafael Krux, etc.) survives at the Internet Archive mirror https://archive.org/details/freepd (~1,000+ MP3s, bulk ZIP/torrent, no account needed). FreePD's entire model was CC0/public-domain dedication, so composition AND recording rights are both waived. Caveat: the mirror is a third-party upload, so spot-check provenance of any track you ship (most are trivially traceable to MacLeod/Teoh). Mood fits: FreePD's old 'Epic/Dramatic' and 'Scoring' categories contained exactly the low-drone tension beds a war-room UI wants.
findings.license_or_source: CC0 1.0 (public domain dedication) — no attribution, commercial OK. Source: freepd.com closure page + archive.org/details/freepd
findings.recommendation: USE — best zero-obligation bulk source, but download from the archive.org mirror and keep a provenance note per track. Do not link players/docs to freepd.com anymore.

findings.name: Kevin MacLeod / Incompetech — top pick for jazz noir
findings.detail: Verified on incompetech.com: two paths — free under Creative Commons Attribution 4.0 (credit required, commercial use explicitly fine), or a flat US$30 per-track no-attribution 'Standard License' (https://incompetech.com/music/royalty-free/faq.html). Direct MP3 download, no account. Required credit format is generated on the site (typically: '"Track" Kevin MacLeod (incompetech.com), Licensed under Creative Commons: By Attribution 4.0'). Specific tracks verified to exist and fit the brief exactly: 'Covert Affair' (film-noir espionage jazz, https://incompetech.com — also mirrored on Wikimedia Commons under CC-BY 3.0: https://commons.wikimedia.org/wiki/Category:Jazz_music_from_Incompetech), 'Deadly Roulette' (gumshoe mystery jazz, https://incompetech.com/wordpress/2016/06/deadly-roulette/), 'Spy Glass' ('super cool jazz for your hardcore detectives', explicitly described as 1950s-settable, https://incompetech.com/wordpress/2015/09/1492/), plus 'Hard Boiled'. His browser also filters by Feel = Dark/Mysterious for orchestral tension beds.
findings.license_or_source: CC BY 4.0 (free, credit required) or $30/track no-attribution license. Source: incompetech.com/music/royalty-free/licenses/ and /faq.html
findings.recommendation: USE — the single best fit for the jazz-noir layer. Budget option: ship CC-BY with a credits screen entry; if you'd rather have zero attribution obligations, $30/track is cheap insurance. His music is ubiquitous — consider it for menus/lounge radio, not your signature main theme.

findings.name: Musopen — go via its CC0 Kickstarter recordings on archive.org, not the website
findings.detail: Musopen.org itself blocks automated access (HTTP 403) and its free tier is account-gated with a 5-downloads/day cap. Critically, licenses are MIXED per recording: PD, CC0, CC BY-SA, and some marked non-commercial — you must check the rights badge on each individual RECORDING page, because composition being PD (pre-1929 published) says nothing about the performance's rights. The clean path: 'Musopen Kickstarter Recordings' on Internet Archive, https://archive.org/details/MusopenKickstarterRecordings — explicitly CC0 1.0 Universal, 2.2 GB ZIP, no account, containing pro recordings of Beethoven/Mozart and the symphony project (Beethoven, Brahms, Tchaikovsky, Sibelius were the campaign targets per https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Musopen). The 'Set Chopin Free' project (https://www.kickstarter.com/projects/Musopen/set-chopin-free) put ~245 Chopin pieces into the public domain in 24-bit audio. Mood picks: Beethoven Symphony No. 7 mvt II (Allegretto) — the canonical grim-processional tension cue; Chopin Prelude Op. 28 No. 4 in E minor and the darker nocturnes for late-night war-room melancholy.
findings.license_or_source: Mixed on musopen.org (PD / CC0 / CC BY-SA / some NC — verify per recording); the archive.org Kickstarter collection is CC0 1.0. Sources: musopen.org/faq/, archive.org/details/MusopenKickstarterRecordings
findings.recommendation: USE the archive.org CC0 collections; treat musopen.org itself as a browsing catalog and verify recording-level rights before shipping anything from it. Never assume 'PD composition = PD recording'.

findings.name: Free Music Archive — usable but a per-track licensing minefield
findings.detail: FMA hosts the full CC spectrum: CC0, BY, BY-SA, BY-ND, BY-NC, BY-NC-SA, BY-NC-ND, plus a retired FMA-Limited license (https://freemusicarchive.org/License_Guide). Only CC0 and CC BY are clean for a commercial game. NC variants are flatly unusable; SA variants are risky (arguable copyleft contamination when synced into a game); ND is risky too (looping/editing/ducking a track arguably creates a derivative). FMA is now owned by Tribe of Noise, which upsells commercial licenses — don't be confused into thinking you need one for CC-BY tracks (you don't). Best artist for this game: Kai Engel — dark neoclassical piano/ambient, most albums CC BY: 'Irsen's Tale' (https://freemusicarchive.org/music/Kai_Engel/Irsens_Tale, also CC-mirrored at https://archive.org/details/Irsens_Tale-14891), 'Sustains' (https://freemusicarchive.org/music/Kai_Engel/Sustains), 'Idea' (https://freemusicarchive.org/music/Kai_Engel/Idea) — exactly the sparse, cold, mournful piano-and-strings bed for a Tension meter creeping upward. A few Kai Engel albums carry NC terms, so check each album's badge.
findings.license_or_source: Mixed CC licenses; verify the badge on every track page. Source: freemusicarchive.org/License_Guide
findings.recommendation: USE selectively — filter to CC0/CC-BY only, screenshot or archive each track's license page at download time (FMA license metadata has historically churned). Kai Engel's CC-BY albums are the standout catch here.

findings.name: OpenGameArt.org — best game-native browsing, no account needed
findings.detail: Verified via the OGA FAQ: five license families — CC0, CC-BY 3.0/4.0, CC-BY-SA, GPL 2/3, and OGA-BY 3.0/4.0 (OGA's own fork of CC-BY that removes the anti-DRM clause, making it safer for Steam/console/App Store distribution than stock CC-BY). No account required to download; the site has a license filter in search. For a commercial game: CC0 and OGA-BY are cleanest, CC-BY fine with credits, avoid GPL and CC-BY-SA music entirely (copyleft on game audio is a legal gray zone not worth touching). Curated collections matching the brief: 'CC0 - Dark Music' (https://opengameart.org/content/cc0-dark-music), 'CC0 - Cinematic Music' (https://opengameart.org/content/cc0-cinematic-music), and 'Good CC0 Music' (https://opengameart.org/content/good-cc0-music) — containing tracks like 'High Alert', 'Laments of the War', and 'Society In Ruins' that suit escalation/crisis states. Quality is uneven; expect to audition heavily.
findings.license_or_source: Per-asset: CC0 / CC-BY / OGA-BY safe; CC-BY-SA and GPL flagged risky for commercial. Source: opengameart.org/content/faq
findings.recommendation: USE for CC0 tension/ambient filler and crisis stingers; filter search to CC0 + OGA-BY + CC-BY. OGA auto-generates a CREDITS.TXT for collections, which makes attribution bookkeeping painless.

findings.name: Pixabay Audio — free and attribution-free, but a bespoke license with real quirks
findings.detail: Verified at https://pixabay.com/service/license-summary/: the Pixabay Content License (NOT CC0 since 2019, and older CC0-era content was re-termed) allows commercial use with no attribution. Quirks that matter: (1) you may not redistribute content 'on a standalone basis' — music embedded in a game with creative effort applied is fine, but shipping the raw tracks in an easily-extractable form (e.g., a plain /music folder of unmodified MP3s) skirts the line; (2) the summary page explicitly warns 'certain Content may be subject to additional intellectual property rights' and puts verification burden on YOU — Pixabay does not meaningfully vet uploads and offers no indemnity, and the audio section has a growing share of AI-generated and misattributed uploads; (3) only the full legal terms are binding, not the summary. Practical mood searches: pixabay.com/music/search/noir%20jazz/, /search/cold%20war/, /search/dark%20ambient%20tension/.
findings.license_or_source: Pixabay Content License (proprietary; commercial OK, no attribution, no standalone redistribution, no indemnity). Source: pixabay.com/service/license-summary/
findings.recommendation: USE WITH CAUTION — fine as a supplementary source, but prefer established uploaders with real portfolios, save a dated copy of the license page, and pack audio in your game's asset archive rather than as loose files. Do not rely on it for signature tracks.

findings.name: YouTube Audio Library — mostly UNUSABLE for a shipped game
findings.detail: Verified via https://support.google.com/youtube/answer/3376882 plus secondary analyses: the standard YouTube Audio Library license is scoped to content you create for YouTube — the terms and support docs do not grant use in off-platform commercial products like a video game, and YouTube explicitly disclaims guidance for off-platform use. The only clean subset is the tracks individually marked Creative Commons (CC-BY 4.0), which are valid anywhere with attribution — but that subset has shrunk over the years, and downloading requires a Google account via YouTube Studio (no anonymous direct download, no API). Net: the convenience is illusory for game dev.
findings.license_or_source: YouTube Audio Library license (platform-scoped, risky off-YouTube) / small CC-BY 4.0 subset (usable). Source: support.google.com/youtube/answer/3376882
findings.recommendation: SKIP for the game itself. At most, mine the CC-BY-flagged subset — but everything there is findable through better-documented channels. Fine for the game's trailer on YouTube, ironically.

findings.name: US military band recordings — genuinely public domain, perfect period flavor
findings.detail: Recordings made by US government employees in the course of duty (US Marine Band 'The President's Own', US Army Band, etc.) are public domain under 17 U.S.C. §105 — no copyright in works of the US government. The Marine Band even publishes an explicit public-domain letter for its 'Complete Marches of John Philip Sousa' project (https://www.marineband.marines.mil/Portals/175/Docs/Audio/Complete%20Marches%20of%20JPS/Sousa%20Marches_Public%20Domain%20letter.pdf) — pro-quality modern recordings of all ~120 Sousa marches, free direct download from marineband.marines.mil, no account. The double-PD check still applies: the recording is PD as a government work, but the COMPOSITION performed must also be PD or licensed — Sousa (d. 1932, works published pre-1929) is fully clear; a government band playing a 1955 copyrighted composition is NOT clear. Also useful: Library of Congress audio collections (https://www.loc.gov/audio/?fa=partof:patriotic+melodies) and the 9 US Army Band Sousa tracks mirrored at partnersinrhyme.com. Fit note: these are marches, not tension beds — ideal as diegetic radio broadcasts, victory-parade cues, superpower anthem flavor, or a warped/detuned 'civilization in decay' motif, less so for the ambient dread layer.
findings.license_or_source: Public domain (17 U.S.C. §105 government works) — verify the underlying composition is also PD (pre-1929 published, e.g., Sousa). Source: marineband.marines.mil PD letter
findings.recommendation: USE for period/diegetic flavor — a crackly-radio-filtered Marine Band Sousa march under a DEFCON escalation screen is exactly the mood. Zero attribution required; credit anyway as good practice ('Performed by the United States Marine Band').

findings.name: Scott Buckley — modern CC-BY cinematic, strong for the dread/orchestral layer
findings.detail: Verified at https://www.scottbuckley.com.au/library/: entire library released Creative Commons Attribution 4.0, commercial use allowed, free direct downloads (WAV/MP3), no account. Production quality is well above typical free-library fare. Fitting tracks visible on the library page: 'Eyes In The Void' (dark chaotic gothic-orchestral march — late-game high-Tension state), 'Unraveling' (slow ambient grief strings — post-crisis aftermath), 'Simulacra' (hybrid orchestral action — hot-war escalation). Attribution: credit 'Scott Buckley' per track (he provides suggested credit text with each download).
findings.license_or_source: CC BY 4.0, commercial OK, credit required. Source: scottbuckley.com.au/library/
findings.recommendation: USE for the cinematic orchestral tension tier that CC0 libraries rarely deliver at quality. One credits-screen line covers it.

findings.name: TRAP: authentic 1950s commercial recordings are NOT public domain
findings.detail: Counterintuitive but critical for a 1950-start game: under the Music Modernization Act's schedule, US sound recordings published 1947–1956 stay protected for 110 years (entering PD ~2058 at the earliest); 1957–Feb 1972 recordings are locked until 2067. As of 2026, only recordings published through ~1926 are PD. So actual period jazz/orchestral 78s and LPs from the era — including much of what circulates on Internet Archive's Great 78 Project (currently the subject of major-label litigation) — are unshippable. Every 'authentic 1950s' sound in the game must instead be a modern PD/CC0/CC-BY recording processed to sound period (vinyl crackle, AM-radio bandpass, tape wow) — or a PD-recording of a PD composition (pre-1929 works via Musopen/military bands).
findings.license_or_source: Music Modernization Act (CLASSICS Act) term schedule; Great 78 Project litigation risk
findings.recommendation: AVOID any rip of an actual 1950s-era commercial recording regardless of how 'old' it feels. Fake the period sonically with DSP over cleanly-licensed modern recordings — cheaper, safer, and you control the mix.

key_takeaways: Recommended stack: (1) jazz noir — Kevin MacLeod CC-BY 4.0 ('Covert Affair', 'Deadly Roulette', 'Spy Glass', 'Hard Boiled'), or pay $30/track to drop attribution; (2) ambient dread/piano — Kai Engel's CC-BY albums on FMA ('Irsen's Tale', 'Sustains'); (3) cinematic tension — Scott Buckley CC-BY 4.0 ('Eyes In The Void', 'Unraveling'); (4) zero-obligation filler — FreePD mirror and OGA CC0 collections; (5) period diegetic flavor — public-domain US Marine Band Sousa recordings through a radio-filter DSP chain.

Breaking news the team likely doesn't know: FreePD.com shut down (site now shows a closure notice) — its CC0 catalog survives at archive.org/details/freepd; and Musopen.org is account-gated/rate-limited, but its Kickstarter recordings are CC0 on archive.org with no account needed.

License triage: CC0 and OGA-BY = ship freely; CC-BY = ship with a credits screen (keep exact track/artist/license/URL per track); CC-BY-SA, any NC variant, GPL music, ND tracks, and the standard YouTube Audio Library license = do not ship. Pixabay's bespoke license is commercial-OK but unvetted-content risk means supplementary use only.

The recording/composition split is the recurring trap: a PD composition (pre-1929 published) can have a fully-copyrighted 2010 recording, and a PD government-band recording can perform a copyrighted composition — both rights must clear. Corollary: NO genuine 1950s commercial recording is public domain until the late 2050s (MMA 110-year term), so all 'period' audio must be modern clean-licensed recordings aged with DSP.

Process rigor for commercial shipping: at download time, archive each track's license page (screenshot or Wayback save), maintain a CREDITS/licenses.toml in the repo mapping every audio asset to source URL + license + required credit text, and prefer sources with no account/API friction (Incompetech, OGA, archive.org, marineband.marines.mil, scottbuckley.com.au all allow anonymous direct download).

reports.topic: Free, commercially shippable sound effects sources + Bevy 0.19 audio stack (bevy_audio vs bevy_kira_audio) for a Cold War grand strategy game

findings.name: Kenney.nl — Interface Sounds pack (top pick for UI clicks)
findings.detail: https://kenney.nl/assets/interface-sounds — 100 sounds tagged interface/click/button. Verified on the asset page as Creative Commons CC0. This is the best single drop-in for map pings, button clicks, and confirm/cancel blips; the dry, clean character suits a restrained war-room UI (pitch/EQ them darker to match the slate-and-brass aesthetic).
findings.license_or_source: CC0 (verified on kenney.nl asset page)
findings.recommendation: Ship it. No credits needed. Start here for all generic UI interactions.

findings.name: Kenney.nl — UI Audio pack (second UI set)
findings.detail: https://kenney.nl/assets/ui-audio — 50 files (buttons, switches, clicks), released 2012. Verified CC0 on the asset page. Kenney's full audio catalog is at https://kenney.nl/assets/category:Audio; other relevant packs for this game: 'Digital Audio' (https://kenney.nl/assets/digital-audio — good raw material for teletype-ish blips and radio-tuner beeps) and 'Sci-fi Sounds' (https://kenney.nl/assets/sci-fi-sounds — alarm/klaxon-adjacent tones). All Kenney assets are published CC0, but the two UI packs above are the ones I license-verified on their individual pages.
findings.license_or_source: CC0 (verified for UI Audio and Interface Sounds; Kenney publishes site-wide CC0)
findings.recommendation: Ship. Use UI Audio + Interface Sounds together; process (lowpass, slight tape saturation) so they don't sound 'mobile game'.

findings.name: Freesound.org — best source for the period-specific sounds (teletype, Geiger, radio static, paper), but requires per-file license discipline
findings.detail: Freesound hosts three licenses: CC0, CC-BY (credit required), CC-BY-NC (NOT usable commercially) — verified on https://freesound.org/help/faq/. An account/login IS required to download sounds via the website. The advanced search UI lets you filter by license — always filter to CC0 (or CC-BY if you keep a credits file). API (https://freesound.org/docs/api/): basic calls need an API key/token; downloading ORIGINAL files additionally requires OAuth2; preview MP3s are downloadable with just the token — for actually shipping audio you want originals, so plan for OAuth2 or just download by hand. This is where you'll find authentic teletype machines, Geiger counters, shortwave static, and paper shuffles that Kenney doesn't cover.
findings.license_or_source: Per-file CC0 / CC-BY / CC-BY-NC (verified on freesound.org FAQ and API docs)
findings.recommendation: Use with CC0 filter applied. Keep a spreadsheet of filename → author → URL → license for every download; treat any CC-BY-NC hit as unusable.

findings.name: OpenGameArt.org — per-asset licenses, filter to CC0; concrete pack: '100 CC0 SFX'
findings.detail: OGA licensing is per-asset (CC0, CC-BY, CC-BY-SA, GPL — the SA/GPL ones are risky for a closed-source commercial game). Verified pack: '100 CC0 SFX' by rubberduck (https://opengameart.org/content/100-cc0-sfx), confirmed CC0 on the page — includes paper, switches, machines, metal, hits: good foley raw material for document-shuffle and mechanical console sounds. Also relevant but license NOT yet verified by me: 'Keyboard Soundpack #1 [Typing and Single Keystrokes]' (https://opengameart.org/content/keyboard-soundpack-1-typing-and-single-keystrokes — 10 typing loops + 32 single keypresses, ideal for the typewriter/teletype motif; check its license box before shipping). Use OGA's search with the license filter set to CC0.
findings.license_or_source: Per-asset; 100 CC0 SFX verified CC0; keyboard pack license unverified — check on page
findings.recommendation: Secondary source after Kenney/Freesound. Avoid CC-BY-SA and GPL-licensed audio entirely.

findings.name: Sonniss GameAudioGDC bundles — huge pro-quality library, custom royalty-free license (not CC0)
findings.detail: https://sonniss.com/gameaudiogdc — verified on the page: royalty-free, commercial use allowed, NO attribution required, license is perpetual across unlimited projects. Restrictions: cannot redistribute/resell the sounds as standalone files or in sound libraries (shipping inside a finished game is explicitly fine); AI/ML training use prohibited. Bundles from 2015–2024, tens of GB each (2024 bundle is 9 zip parts). These are professional recordings — by far the highest production quality in the free tier; excellent hunting ground for klaxons, radio interference, mechanical rooms, ambience beds.
findings.license_or_source: Sonniss royalty-free license (verified on sonniss.com/gameaudiogdc) — commercial OK, no attribution, no standalone redistribution
findings.recommendation: Use for hero sounds (DEFCON-shift klaxon, nuclear-alert stingers, ambience). Archive the license text alongside your assets since it's a custom license, not CC.

findings.name: Pixabay SFX — usable but proprietary license, weakest provenance
findings.detail: https://pixabay.com/sound-effects/ under the Pixabay Content License (https://pixabay.com/service/license-summary/ — verified): commercial use allowed, no attribution required, NOT CC0; forbids standalone redistribution and warns 'certain Content may be subject to additional intellectual property rights.' Pixabay is user-uploaded with lighter curation than Freesound, so provenance risk (someone uploading sounds they don't own) is the real issue for a commercial title.
findings.license_or_source: Pixabay Content License (proprietary, verified) — commercial OK, no attribution, not CC0
findings.recommendation: Third-tier fallback only. Prefer Freesound CC0 for anything you can find in both places.

findings.name: BBC Sound Effects archive — FLAGGED: do not ship
findings.detail: https://sound-effects.bbcrewind.co.uk has thousands of authentic Cold War-era recordings (teleprinters, sirens, newsroom ambience) that look perfect for this game, but its free downloads are governed by the RemArc licence, which historically permits personal/educational/non-commercial use only; commercial use requires a paid Pro license. I could not re-verify the license page this session (it wouldn't load), which is itself a reason for caution.
findings.license_or_source: RemArc licence (non-commercial) — unverified this session, treat as NC
findings.recommendation: Do NOT ship BBC archive sounds in a commercial game without buying their commercial license. Use only as a reference for the sonic palette.

findings.name: Bevy 0.19 built-in audio (bevy_audio 0.19.1) — fine for one-shot UI SFX, no crossfade or loop points
findings.detail: Verified on docs.rs (bevy_audio 0.19.1, published 2026-08-13): built on rodio 0.22. Cargo features (verified on docs.rs/crate/bevy/latest/features): 'vorbis' (OGG) is on by default via the 'audio' default feature; optional: 'mp3', 'flac', 'wav', 'aac', 'mp4', plus an 'audio-all-formats' convenience feature and symphonia-backed decoders as 'symphonia-flac', 'symphonia-vorbis', 'symphonia-wav'. API: spawn an entity with AudioPlayer(handle) + PlaybackSettings (PlaybackMode::Once/Loop/Despawn, per-source Volume); control live playback via the AudioSink component; GlobalVolume resource for master volume. There is NO built-in crossfading, no tweened volume transitions, and no intro-then-loop points — you'd hand-roll fades by mutating AudioSink volume every frame.
findings.license_or_source: docs.rs/bevy_audio 0.19.1 and bevy 0.19.1 feature list (verified)
findings.recommendation: Sufficient if the game only ever plays one music track and fire-and-forget SFX; insufficient for the moody crossfading soundtrack this game wants.

findings.name: bevy_kira_audio 0.26 — supports Bevy 0.19; use it. Channels + tweened fades + loop points
findings.detail: Verified on the GitHub README (github.com/NiklasEi/bevy_kira_audio): compatibility table maps Bevy 0.19 → bevy_kira_audio 0.26 (0.18 → 0.25, 0.17 → 0.24) — note the crate's own version numbers do NOT track Bevy's (bevy_kira_audio 0.19.0 is an old 2024 release for Bevy 0.13; don't be fooled by matching numbers). Features: typed audio channels (add_audio_channel::<MusicChannel>()) with independent volume/panning/playback-rate; smooth transitions on every change via AudioTween + AudioEasing (this is your crossfade primitive: fade_out on the old track's channel, fade_in on the new); loop points including play-intro-once-then-loop (ideal for a tension-tiered soundtrack); formats OGG (default), MP3, FLAC, WAV via feature flags; RON settings loader; works on web builds. Important integration note from the README: it REPLACES bevy_audio — add bevy with default-features minus 'audio' (e.g. disable the 'audio'/'vorbis' default) so rodio and kira don't both grab the output device.
findings.license_or_source: github.com/NiklasEi/bevy_kira_audio README + crates.io versions (verified; crate itself MIT/Apache-2.0 dual-licensed as is standard in the Bevy ecosystem)
findings.recommendation: Adopt bevy_kira_audio = "0.26" now. Pattern: one MusicChannel (looping beds, crossfade on Tension-tier changes via fade_out/fade_in with ~2-4s AudioTween), one AmbienceChannel (radio static / room tone, volume tied to the Tension meter), one UiChannel (one-shot clicks/pings, no tween). Keep master/music/sfx sliders as per-channel volume, not GlobalVolume.

findings.name: Practical Bevy pattern for this game (crossfade + UI SFX)
findings.detail: Cargo.toml: bevy = { version = "0.19", default-features = false, features = [everything you use EXCEPT audio/vorbis] }; bevy_kira_audio = { version = "0.26", features = ["ogg"] } — standardize shipped assets on OGG Vorbis (small, patent-free, default decode path in both stacks; keep WAV only for very short UI clicks if latency ever matters). Define marker structs MusicChannel/UiChannel/AmbienceChannel, register with app.add_audio_channel::<T>(); play music with channel.play(handle).looped().fade_in(AudioTween::new(Duration::from_secs(3), AudioEasing::OutPowi(2))); on a Tension-tier crossfade, call channel.stop().fade_out(tween) then play the next track with a matching fade_in (or use two music channels and alternate for true overlapping crossfade). UI SFX: a system reading click/hover events that calls ui_channel.play(handle) — pre-load handles at startup into a Resource so first-click isn't delayed by asset load. Tie AmbienceChannel volume to the Tension meter each frame with a tweened set_volume for the 'room gets tenser' effect (e.g., Geiger-tick bed that only becomes audible above high tension).
findings.license_or_source: Derived from verified bevy_kira_audio 0.26 README API + bevy 0.19 feature list
findings.recommendation: Implement channels + preloaded SFX handles from day one; retrofitting channel routing after sounds are scattered through systems is painful.

key_takeaways: Core SFX plan: Kenney 'Interface Sounds' (100 sounds) + 'UI Audio' (50 sounds), both verified CC0, cover clicks/pings/buttons with zero obligations; period flavor (teletype, Geiger counter, shortwave static, paper shuffles) comes from Freesound.org with the license filter locked to CC0 — Freesound requires a login to download, and its API needs a key plus OAuth2 for original-quality files, so manual downloads are simpler for a small asset set.

License triage, verified on source pages: CC0 (Kenney, filtered Freesound/OGA) = ship freely; CC-BY = fine with a credits file; Sonniss GDC bundles = royalty-free commercial with no attribution but a custom license (archive its text; no standalone redistribution; pro quality — best free source for klaxons/stingers); Pixabay = commercially usable but proprietary license with weaker provenance, use as last resort; BBC Sound Effects archive = non-commercial RemArc license, do NOT ship despite being thematically perfect.
Maintain a per-file provenance manifest (file, source URL, author, license) from the first sound onward — it is the only way licensing rigor survives to a commercial release.

Bevy 0.19's built-in bevy_audio (rodio 0.22; OGG/vorbis by default, mp3/flac/wav/aac behind feature flags, symphonia-* decoder features available) handles one-shot SFX and global volume but has no crossfading, tweening, or loop points.

Use bevy_kira_audio 0.26 — it explicitly supports Bevy 0.19 (its version numbers do NOT track Bevy's: 0.19→0.26 per the README table) and provides exactly what a Tension-driven soundtrack needs: typed channels, AudioTween fade_in/fade_out for crossfades, and intro-then-loop points; you must disable Bevy's default 'audio' feature since it replaces bevy_audio.

Recommended architecture: three channels (Music with 2-4s tweened crossfades keyed to Tension tiers, Ambience with volume driven by the Tension meter — e.g., a Geiger-tick bed fading in at high tension, UI with preloaded one-shot handles), all assets shipped as OGG Vorbis.

reports.topic: Audio direction for a Cold War grand strategy game (RTwP, 0-100 Tension meter, war-room aesthetic): lessons from DEFCON, Paradox, FTL/Balatro, Twilight Struggle, Fallout/TNO, plus license-verified asset sourcing

findings.name: DEFCON: the reference point — dread through restraint and ambiguity
findings.detail: DEFCON (Introversion; audio by Alistair Lindsay & Michael Maidment) is the single best model for this game. Its soundscape is a bunker, not a battlefield: drifting ambient instrumentation mingled with computer hum, the hollow wash of recycled air, indistinguishable radio chatter, faint coughing — and sounds ambiguous enough that players ask 'is that someone crying?' Chris Delay said they 'spent a huge amount of time trying to create the atmosphere of being buried deep within an underground bunker, slowly ending the world.' Three transferable principles: (1) AMBIGUITY — the famous 'muffled sobs' work because they are barely audible and never confirmed; the player's imagination authors the horror. (2) COLD DETACHMENT AS CONTRAST — megadeath events get small, clinical sounds (a soft tone, a counter ticking up), and the gap between sound and meaning is the horror. (3) THE ROOM IS THE INSTRUMENT — everything is filtered as if heard through concrete and ventilation; nothing is 'close-mic'd'. Sources: https://blog.codinghorror.com/defcon-shall-we-play-a-game/ , https://www.escapistmagazine.com/everybody-dies-in-defcon/ , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/DEFCON_(video_game)
findings.license_or_source: Design analysis only — do not reuse DEFCON audio (commercial copyright, Introversion).
findings.recommendation: Adopt DEFCON's bunker-perspective mixing as the game's core identity: the player is IN a war room hearing the world second-hand. Low-pass everything diegetic; keep the most terrible events the quietest. One deliberately ambiguous human sound (a distant cough, a chair creak, one unconfirmed sob at Brink) is worth more than any orchestral hit.

findings.name: Paradox (HoI4/EU4): weighted-shuffle playlists with state-conditioned tracks — good rotation model, weak moment-to-moment reactivity
findings.detail: Verified from HoI4's own music scripting (https://hoi4.paradoxwikis.com/Music_modding): tracks are chosen by weighted shuffle where each song has a chance block with base/factor/add modifiers gated on game state — e.g. 'modifier = { factor = 0 has_war = no }' silences a track in peacetime. This gives cheap, robust macro-reactivity (peace playlist vs war playlist, country/faction weighting) without any audio-engine cleverness, and it's trivially reimplementable in Bevy: give each track a weight function over game state (tension band, war status, decade) and re-roll on track end. Waldetoft's HoI4 score gives each faction a distinct sound blended with battle ambience (dev diary 51: https://forum.paradoxplaza.com/forum/threads/hearts-of-iron-iv-development-diary-51-music-sound-design.919038/ , soundtrack: https://open.spotify.com/album/2EhDqRjaxd6HCdTu3PikCt). The weakness to NOT copy: Paradox music is a non-diegetic concert playlist that rarely acknowledges the current moment — a crisis can fire during a jaunty track. Their fix is DLC 'radio stations'; ours should be actual reactivity.
findings.license_or_source: Design analysis; HoI4 wiki documents the moddable system publicly.
findings.recommendation: Use the weighted-shuffle-with-state-triggers pattern as the OUTER layer (which composition plays), but gate every track to a tension band so a wrong-mood track can never play. Add a 2-4s 'duck and stinger' interrupt channel for events, which Paradox lacks at the moment level.

findings.name: FTL / Into the Breach / Balatro: vertical layering maps directly onto a 0-100 tension meter
findings.detail: FTL (Ben Prunty) is the cleanest published example: most tracks exist as an Explore and a Battle version — same harmony and tempo, the Battle mix adds percussion and intensity — and the game CROSSFADES between the two stems in real time (https://www.pcgamer.com/ftl-faster-than-light-soundtrack-ben-prunty/ , https://ftl.fandom.com/wiki/Soundtrack). Balatro (LouisF) generalizes this to 5 simultaneous synced layers of one 7/4 composition, mixed against game state so music never restarts, only thickens (https://balatrowiki.org/w/Music). This is exactly the right architecture for a continuous 0-100 Tension meter: author ONE piece per era/theatre as 3-4 stems that are always playing in sync, and drive stem gains from tension — no transition logic, no musical seams, and RTwP pause can simply low-pass and duck the whole bus rather than stop it. Into the Breach (Ben Prunty again) shows the per-region variant: each island has its own palette so long sessions don't fatigue.
findings.license_or_source: Design analysis; technique is not protectable, implement freely.
findings.recommendation: Commission/produce each score cue as synced stems: Layer A drone/pads (always on), Layer B pulse (clock ticks, low ostinato, fades in ~30 tension), Layer C strings/brass tension figures (~60), Layer D pressure layer — heartbeat-adjacent percussion, cluster swells (~85). Tension meter drives a smoothed gain curve per layer in Bevy (bevy_audio/kira supports per-track volume tweening; kira is the better fit for stem sync).

findings.name: Twilight Struggle digital: the cautionary tale — cheap period pastiche reads as cheap
findings.detail: The Playdek adaptation has ambient music and event-triggered sounds, but players specifically complained the reworked soundtrack sounded like stock MIDI samples with 'wailing trumpets and military drums' that got annoying fast, and asked for the old, shadowier music back (https://steamcommunity.com/app/406290/discussions/0/154644045363584608/ , https://www.play-board-games.com/twilight-struggle-digital-review/). Lesson: a Cold War theme invites lazy signifiers (snare drums, trumpet fanfares, Soviet-choir pastiche). Done with cheap sample libraries it actively damages the tone. The original TS track worked because it was shadowy and tense, not martial. Also note the community instinct: BGG's 'ultimate Twilight Struggle soundtrack' thread reaches for real period gravity, not military kitsch (https://boardgamegeek.com/thread/1327344/the-ultimate-twilight-struggle-soundtrack).
findings.license_or_source: Design analysis.
findings.recommendation: Ban fanfares, marching snares, and faux-Red-Army choirs from the main palette. If budget forces a small palette, choose DEFCON-style electronics + treated piano/strings over orchestral mockups — sparse synthesis ages far better than fake orchestra.

findings.name: Fallout-style 1950s needle-drops are OFF THE TABLE without real licensing budget — verified by statute
findings.detail: Fallout's identity leans on licensed period records, and even Bethesda-scale money hits walls: Interplay could not clear 'I Don't Want to Set the World on Fire' for Fallout 1 and substituted 'Maybe'; the song's rights are split across multiple publishers and heirs, some unlocatable (https://fallout.fandom.com/wiki/I_Don%27t_Want_to_Set_the_World_on_Fire , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/I_Don%27t_Want_to_Set_the_World_on_Fire). The statutory reality (verified): under the Music Modernization Act/CLASSICS Act, US sound recordings published 1947-1956 are protected for 110 years — a 1950 record stays locked until 2061 (https://www.copyright.gov/music-modernization/pre1972-soundrecordings/ , https://publicdomainreview.org/blog/2021/12/all-sound-recordings-prior-to-1923-will-enter-the-us-public-domain-in-2022 , https://library.mi.edu/musiccopyright/duration). Every 1950s needle-drop requires BOTH a master license and a composition sync license. The legal loophole that DOES exist: recordings published before 1926 are now PD (pre-1923 entered PD in 2022; 1923-1925 followed through 2026), and compositions published before 1931 are PD — so 1920s 78rpm records of 1920s songs are fully clear, and in a 1950 setting they read plausibly as 'old records' on a wireless.
findings.license_or_source: US Copyright Office / MMA schedule, verified. Pre-1926 78s on Internet Archive's George Blood collection are the practical source; check each item's date and rights field.
findings.recommendation: Skip 1950s pop entirely. If you want diegetic radio music, use verified pre-1926 78rpm recordings (crackle included, free character) or commission original pastiche in period style — a newly composed 'crooner on shortwave' is 100% yours. Never assume 'old = public domain' for recordings.

findings.name: The New Order (TNO) mod: original score keyed to narrative states, and the superevent stinger pattern
findings.detail: TNO ships 50+ ORIGINAL tracks by its own composer team (Ayden George and the TNO dev team — https://steamcommunity.com/sharedfiles/filedetails/?id=2213783261 , https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=DqNp8eg6JkU), precisely because HoI4's licensed score didn't fit its bleak tone and because original music is the only clean licensing path for a distributed mod. Its most-imitated device is the SUPEREVENT: gameplay halts, a full-screen card appears, and a dedicated musical stinger plays (nuclear exchange, leader death). Players remember these moments as the mod's identity. That is the strongest argument that a grand strategy game's audio budget should be spent on a small number of scripted, high-impact moments rather than spread evenly.
findings.license_or_source: Design analysis; TNO's music is the team's original work, not reusable.
findings.recommendation: Build 6-10 bespoke stingers for irreversible historical moments (first Soviet bomb test, war declaration between superpowers, first nuclear use, DEFCON-1/Brink entry, armistice). Duck all other audio, play the stinger, let silence follow. Silence AFTER a stinger is the payoff — do not resume music for 10-20 seconds.

findings.name: Numbers stations: The Conet Project is a licensing trap — synthesize your own
findings.detail: The obvious asset grab — Irdial-Discs' Conet Project recordings of Cold War numbers stations — is actively enforced: Irdial sued Wilco over a ~90-second 'Yankee Hotel Foxtrot' sample and Wilco settled, paying royalties and Irdial's legal fees (https://www.rollingstone.com/music/music-news/wilco-settle-sample-suit-244171/ , https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Conet_Project). Irdial claims recording copyright (UK law protects the recordist even of unauthored broadcasts); their 'free music' distribution has never been a commercial-use grant. However, the CONTENT of a numbers station is not protectable style: a filtered synthetic voice reading digit groups, an interval signal (music-box melody like Lincolnshire Poacher's, or a tone), and shortwave artifacts (heterodyne whine, fading, atmospherics) are all trivially synthesizable. TTS or a hired voice through a shortwave DSP chain (band-limit 300-3kHz, AM artifacts, slow fading, noise floor) is indistinguishable from the real thing and 100% owned.
findings.license_or_source: Conet Project: copyright claimed and litigated by Irdial-Discs — treat as unusable/risky for commercial use. Own synthesis: fully clear.
findings.recommendation: Produce original numbers-station loops in-house (Spanish/German/Russian/English voices, digit groups, interval melodies you compose). Use them as a signature Brink-tension element and as flavor when hovering intel/espionage UI. This is cheap, authentic, and legally bulletproof — and dodges the one active litigant in this asset space.

findings.name: Verified-safe asset sources for the era palette
findings.detail: (1) US civil defense material: 'Duck and Cover' (1951, Archer Productions for the Federal Civil Defense Administration) is marked Public Domain on Internet Archive (verified: https://archive.org/details/DuckandC1951); FCDA/US government audio (CONELRAD announcements, civil defense PSAs, atomic test film audio from Prelinger/NARA) is PD as federal work — verify each item's rights field, since some ephemeral films were private productions. (2) EBS/EAS-style attention tones and WWV-style time signals are synthesizable sine tones (853+960 Hz) — no asset needed. (3) Freesound.org: per-sound licenses (CC0, CC-BY, CC-BY-NC — https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Freesound); filter search to CC0 only for teletype, Geiger clicks, tube-radio tuning, rotary phones, switchboard clacks; CC-BY acceptable with a credits screen; treat any CC-BY-NC hit as unusable. (4) Pixabay's content license also allows commercial game use without attribution for SFX (https://pixabay.com/sound-effects/search/cc0/). (5) WARNING on Soviet classical: Shostakovich/Prokofiev/Khachaturian COMPOSITIONS are not PD in the US (URAA-restored, 95 years from publication), so 'just use Soviet symphonies' fails on composition rights even with a PD-licensed performance — Musopen's page could not be verified this session (403), so treat any classical recording as requiring per-item verification of BOTH composition and recording status.
findings.license_or_source: archive.org item pages (verified PD marking on Duck and Cover); Freesound per-sound license model (verified); MMA schedule via copyright.gov (verified); Conet risk (verified via settled litigation).
findings.recommendation: Sourcing policy: CC0/US-gov-PD first, CC-BY with in-game credits second, everything else commissioned. Keep a licensing manifest (asset, source URL, license, date verified, screenshot) from day one — retrofitting provenance is how indies get burned.

findings.name: THE DIRECTION — three tension states of the map, from Calm to Brink
findings.detail: The map is a war room, heard from inside. CALM (0-39): near-silence as a positive aesthetic. Room tone: ventilation hum, faint fluorescent buzz, distant teletype bursts every 30-90s, occasional muffled footsteps beyond a door. Music layer A only — a slow, warm-but-uneasy drone with treated piano (think DEFCON's 'ambient' register, not pastoral). Interactions sound analog and satisfying: relay-click for selections, typewriter strikes for orders, paper slide for panels. GOAL: the player should feel safe enough that any change registers. CRISIS (40-74): the room wakes up. Teletype frequency doubles and occasionally runs long (a 'flash traffic' burst is itself an alarm the player learns to dread). Layer B (a clock-tick/low ostinato pulse) and C (tension strings/brass, dissonant sustained clusters) fade in on the tension curve. A telephone rings — once, unanswered — at threshold crossings. Radio-chatter bed, unintelligible, low in the mix. Pitch/space narrows: slightly more low-pass on the world, as if the doors sealed. BRINK (75-100): inversion — as tension maxes, STRIP the music back rather than piling on. Layer D is a bare pulse (heartbeat-adjacent), sub-bass pressure, and the numbers-station loop bleeding in on shortwave; strings reduce to a single high sustained tone. The muffled-sob move lives here: one distant, unconfirmed human sound, played rarely (roll it, don't loop it). Klaxon NEVER loops — one short alert when entering Brink, then oppressive quiet. At 95+ add faint Geiger clicks tied to nothing, and let the UI sounds themselves go slightly duller. RTwP PAUSE: don't stop audio — low-pass and duck the whole world bus ~6dB, keep the room tone; pause should feel like holding your breath, and unpause like the world rushing back.
findings.license_or_source: Original direction, synthesized from DEFCON/FTL/TNO analysis above.
findings.recommendation: Implement as one always-running stem group per era + a state-driven ambience mixer keyed to the tension value (smoothed, with hysteresis so 74↔75 flicker can't retrigger stingers). Kira (via bevy_kira_audio) over stock bevy_audio for sample-accurate stem sync and tweened gains.

findings.name: THE DIRECTION — menu theme, sound/silence policy, and era touches
findings.detail: MENU: cold open on room tone (2-3s of just the bunker) before music enters — a slow 3-4 minute piece in the game's home key: low strings or synthesized string ensemble, a single treated piano motif (the game's 3-5 note identity motif, reusable in stingers), distant shortwave texture underneath. Mood: 'the meeting before the meeting' — grave, patient, a little beautiful. No percussion, no fanfare. WHAT GETS A SOUND: player orders (typewriter/relay confirm), incoming events (teletype burst, graded: short=minor, long=major, bell-ding=flash), tension threshold crossings (single phone ring / single tone), turn-of-year (soft calendar/page sound), stingers for irreversible moments, UI hover only on high-consequence controls. WHAT STAYS SILENT: unit movement on the map (armies are abstractions — silence keeps the clinical horror), routine AI actions, most notifications (badge silently; sound is a budget, spend it on meaning), combat itself at grand-strategy zoom (a distant rumble at most — DEFCON's lesson: the deaths are numbers, and that should be uncomfortable). ERA-AUTHENTIC TOUCHES (all synthesizable/PD): teletype as the PRIMARY information sound (it is to this game what the Geiger counter is to Fallout); shortwave tuning sweeps when switching map modes or intel views; original numbers-station loops in espionage contexts and at Brink; CONELRAD-style '640/1240' civil defense announcement pastiche (write your own copy, PD-style delivery) in nuclear-crisis events; rotary dial and switchboard sounds in diplomacy UI; WWV-style time pips on autosave or hour-tick at high speed; vacuum-tube warm-up whine when opening the radio/intel panel; period-correct 25Hz/50Hz telephone ring for Moscow-Washington moments (the real hotline was teletype, 1963 — before that, use cables/teletype for authenticity). Voice: avoid full VO; processed, band-limited fragmentary radio voices (own recordings) preserve ambiguity and budget.
findings.license_or_source: Original direction; all era sounds either synthesized in-house, US-gov PD, or Freesound CC0-filtered.
findings.recommendation: Write the sound-or-silence table into the design doc as policy, not vibes: every new feature must argue for WHY it earns a sound. Compose the 3-5 note motif first — it seeds menu, stingers, and numbers-station interval melody, giving audio identity coherence on an indie budget.

findings.name: Pitfalls to avoid
findings.detail: (1) LICENSING: assuming 1950s recordings are PD (they're protected to ~2058-2067 under MMA); grabbing Conet Project audio (litigated); using Soviet classical compositions (URAA-restored); CC-BY-NC or CC-SA assets anywhere in a commercial build; Freesound assets without checking the PER-SOUND license; 'free for personal use' SFX packs. (2) DESIGN: martial pastiche (Twilight Struggle digital's stock-MIDI trumpets — the most-cited flaw of the closest comparable title); looping alarms during crisis (fatigue kills dread — alert once, then silence); scoring everything (if Calm already has strings, Brink has nowhere to go — dynamic range is the whole game for a tension meter); notification sound spam in a grand strategy UI (players WILL mute you, and a muted game has no Brink); restarting music on state change instead of crossfading synced stems (audible seams break the continuous-dread illusion); making nuclear events bombastic (DEFCON proves quiet is scarier); tying audio intensity linearly to tension without hysteresis (meter jitter at a boundary causes audible flapping); shipping without a mixer hierarchy (music/ambience/UI/stinger buses with ducking sidechains — retrofitting this in Bevy mid-project is painful, set up buses in kira on day one).
findings.license_or_source: Synthesis of all verified findings above.
findings.recommendation: Treat the audio like the Tension meter's second display: every design review asks 'can a blindfolded player estimate the tension value within one band?' If yes, the audio is doing its job.

key_takeaways: Steal DEFCON's philosophy wholesale: the player is inside a bunker hearing the world second-hand — restraint, ambiguity (the unconfirmed sob), and clinical quiet for catastrophic events. Quiet IS the horror; reserve near-silence for the Brink, not just for Calm.

Architecture: FTL/Balatro-style synced vertical stems (drone → pulse → strings → pressure) driven by the 0-100 tension meter with smoothing and hysteresis, wrapped in a Paradox-style weighted-shuffle track selector gated by tension band and era; plus 6-10 TNO-style superevent stingers followed by mandatory silence. Use kira (bevy_kira_audio) for stem sync and bus ducking from day one.

Sound is a budget: orders, teletype-graded events, threshold crossings, and stingers get sounds; unit movement, routine notifications, and zoomed-out combat stay silent. Teletype is this game's Geiger counter — the signature information sound.

Licensing (verified on source pages): 1950s recordings are locked until ~2058-2067 (MMA 110-year rule, copyright.gov) — no Fallout-style needle-drops without paid sync+master licenses; Conet Project numbers-station recordings are litigated (Irdial v. Wilco settlement) — synthesize your own numbers stations instead, which is cheap and bulletproof; Soviet classical compositions are URAA-restored, not PD.

Safe sources: US federal civil-defense audio (Duck and Cover verified PD on archive.org), pre-1926 78rpm recordings (recordings pre-1926 + compositions pre-1931 both PD) for plausible 'old records on the radio' in 1950, Freesound filtered to CC0 (check per-sound license; CC-BY ok with credits screen; reject NC/SA), and in-house synthesis for tones (EBS 853+960Hz, time pips, shortwave DSP). Keep a dated licensing manifest per asset from day one.

Anti-patterns proven by comparable titles: Twilight Struggle digital's stock-MIDI martial pastiche is the most-criticized audio in the genre's closest comparable — ban fanfares, marching snares, and faux-Soviet choirs; never loop alarms; never restart music on state change; a menu theme should open on 2-3s of room tone before a sparse, grave string-and-treated-piano piece built on a 3-5 note motif reused across stingers and the numbers-station interval melody.
